extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy writers, and entertainment/industry readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative comments about writing, testing, and performing stand-up and topical comedy (including podcast-as-stand-up and roast conventions) as discussed by a practicing comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability of material (sayable long-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: In stand-up, I try to do things that I can say for a long period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer material that remains performable over long stretches of a career or over tours; evergreen jokes sustain a performer's setlist without needing constant replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshopping with live audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: I wanted to keep my podcast as close to stand-up as possible... There’s a real, live audience. I can see if people laugh or don’t laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test jokes in front of live crowds (even on a podcast) to gauge real-time reaction; use different venues, observe laughter, and prune jokes that don't land. The article emphasizes live testing as central to refining material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative pruning — drop jokes that don't work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the jokes are good and some of them are bad, and I don’t do those ones again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After testing, remove material that consistently fails. Be ruthless in editing your setlist based on audience feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling bad jokes as part of the creative process
rubrics_metrics.description: I have this theory with jokes — that they’re all kind of stacked up in your throat and if you don’t tell the bad ones, they keep the good ones from coming out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some bad bits are necessary experimentation; taking risks and occasionally telling weaker jokes can help unstick better material and generate new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: High output for topical material
rubrics_metrics.description: On my podcast, I do a lot more topical stuff because I’m doing about 40 new minutes of material every week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing a large volume of fresh material (e.g., weekly new minutes) supports topical comedy and rapid iteration; this approach suits formats that prioritize timeliness over long-term durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good jokes illuminate the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: What good jokes do. They illuminate the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong comedy often works by revealing or clarifying underlying truths about people, institutions, or events; aim for insight, not merely shock or insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roast conventions: meanness can be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A roast is mean... she was going to be terribly mean — which I think is fair when you’re doing terribly mean things. It’s also very fair when you’re doing a roast. That’s what a roast is. A roast is mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a roast context, harshness is an expected device and can be justified when the target's actions invite criticism; context and role (roast versus other formats) determine acceptable tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target actions, not appearances (avoid attacking looks)
rubrics_metrics.description: I would still love for someone to explain to me how they thought that joke was making fun of her appearance. Because there’s not a shred of it that says anything about how she looks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of whom or what the joke targets; jokes perceived as attacking appearance risk backlash and may be viewed as unfair. Aim to critique behavior, decisions, or policies rather than physical traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and 'heavy lifting' versus curation
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s not necessarily him doing stand-up. It’s him having other comedians come on — I think they get a minute or two to tell jokes. So basically, he’s just a content curator and he’s not really doing the heavy lifting of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value performers who write and deliver original material ('heavy lifting') over formats or hosts who primarily curate other people's work; originality is a mark of craft and effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence over mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: I think right now we’re in a time where mediocrity is being highlighted because everyone can be mediocre, and not everyone can be excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for well-crafted, standout material rather than joining the noise; widespread accessibility makes mediocrity common, so excellence differentiates performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format fidelity: keep podcast close to stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: I wanted to keep my podcast as close to stand-up as possible... I just made it stand-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a podcast or recorded format is intended to function as stand-up, preserve stand-up conventions (live audience, editing toward performance) rather than converting to freeform rambling; format choices shape audience expectations and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of institutional/political pressures that shape performance choices
rubrics_metrics.description: They didn’t want to make Trump mad... It’s a really, really scary place to be in journalism... a lot harder to do that [call things out] if you don’t want to make that subject mad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that event organizers, institutions, or political contexts may constrain what comics (or journalists) can say; these pressures affect booking decisions and the permissible scope of satire at certain events.
